metadata.title: A New Measure of Skills Mismatch (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses the first wave of the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC), which is based on country-specific household samples designed to be representative of adults aged 16–65, with harmonized sampling procedures for cross-country comparability. The paper restricts the analytic sample to dependent employees holding only one job, and further drops certain occupations (ISCO 0 and 6) and groups ISCO 1 and 2 due to small sample sizes; it also excludes occupations with fewer than 10 self-reported well-matched workers. The paper states that standard errors account for differences in sampling frames across countries and for variation induced by the imputation of ability scores, with details in an appendix, but it does not explicitly name or report the use of specific survey weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight methods. Because the study is not framed as an ML prediction pipeline and does not report a weight variable name, the exact weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are skill-mismatch classifications and skill-use differences derived from PIAAC literacy and numeracy proficiency scores (IRT-based) and self-reported mismatch questions, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. The paper also excludes problem solving due to higher missingness, but it does not explicitly describe a missing-data handling strategy for the remaining variables (e.g., how missing background responses or task-level missingness are treated beyond the stated exclusion). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling details, even though the study does discuss imputation of proficiency scores via an IRT model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIAAC first-wave data for literacy and numeracy; excluded problem solving because of relatively high missingness (about 10% on average, over 20% in some countries). The final working sample is restricted to dependent employees holding only one job. Jobs are defined separately for each country using ISCO 1-digit codes; occupations ISCO 0 (armed forces) and 6 (skilled agricultural and fishery workers) are dropped, and ISCO 1 (managers) and 2 (professionals) are grouped due to small sample sizes. Additionally, occupations with fewer than 10 self-reported well-matched workers are dropped. For mismatch requirement estimation, the paper uses 5th and 95th percentiles within occupation distributions among workers who report neither needing training nor being able to do more demanding jobs, to limit outlier influence.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper proposes a theory-based measure of skills mismatch using PIAAC first-wave data for adults aged 16–65, focusing on literacy and numeracy (problem solving is excluded due to higher missingness). It defines job-specific minimum and maximum skill requirements using self-reported “well-matched” workers and IRT-based proficiency scores, then classifies dependent employees into under-skilled, well-matched, and over-skilled groups. Across the pooled sample, about 86% are well-matched in literacy (4% under-skilled, 10% over-skilled) and similarly for numeracy. The study reports substantial cross-domain overlap (94% of literacy well-matched are also numeracy well-matched; Spearman ρ = 0.81) and subgroup differences by gender, education, age, and foreign status. Methodologically, it does not present ML model performance metrics because the approach is measurement/estimation rather than predictive ML, and it does not explicitly document missing-data handling beyond excluding problem solving and describing IRT-based proficiency imputation.
